Cleaning up and reducing a scan

Load a scan and clean it up — clear the stray islands, delete what is not the part, turn it the right way out, cut off the base it stood on, fill its holes, smooth out the scatter, expand or shrink it, hollow it — and reduce it to a light mesh to model over in CAD, held within a tolerance you set, measured against the scan to prove it, and exported where you aligned it. STL, PLY, OBJ or 3MF, in millimetres — everything stays in this browser.
A light copy of the scan to model over in CAD, held within a tolerance you set — the scan itself stays as it is
Find the specks floating off the scan — every piece joined to nothing else and smaller than a size you set — mark them on the part, and delete them once you say so
Mark surface on the part by hand — a window, a brush or a lasso — and delete it from the scan: a fixture, a clamp, a patch of the table
Turn the surface over so it faces the other way — the whole part, exported inside-out, or a patch you mark that faces in
Cut the scan with a plane and take one side off — the turntable it stood on, or half the part — closing it flat where the plane went through
Close the holes a scanner left, every one smaller than a size you set, with patches that carry the surface across
Take the scanner’s scatter out of the surface, never moving any point further than a limit you set, sharp edges held
Move the surface along its normal by a distance — out or in, the whole part or a marked region — not a scale: a bore gets narrower as the part grows
Take a solid body out of the scan, add it, or keep what the two share — a bore the scanner could not see to the bottom of, cut out with a cylinder modelled in Reverse engineer
Cut a body modelled to mend a broken part to fit the scanned break — the missing piece, to print and glue in
Hollow a closed part, leaving a wall of a thickness you set round a sealed cavity — or thicken an open surface into a solid
